opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say don't start with a physical robot at all. Start in simulation. That's the beauty of this field right now: everything we do begins in simulation anyway. With something like Isaac Gym or Isaac Lab, or MuJoCo-based setups, you can train a quadruped to walk on a single consumer GPU in minutes. There are open-source example environments for robots like ANYmal, Unitree's quadrupeds, and others, so you can clone a repo, hit train, and watch a policy learn to walk. That's how you build intuition: playing with the reward terms, the observations, domain randomization, and seeing what breaks.

When you do want to move to hardware, I'd go with a quadruped rather than a humanoid. Quadrupeds are much more forgiving. They're statically stable when they stand, they don't fall over as easily, and when they do fall they usually don't break. That matters a lot when you're testing policies that might do something crazy the first time. A humanoid falling is a much bigger deal, both for the robot and for whoever's standing nearby.

On the specific choice, the relatively affordable quadrupeds, like the Unitree Go1 and Go2, have made a huge difference. A few years ago you needed a research lab budget to get a capable legged robot. Now a lot of universities and even individuals can buy one, and the community has shared code to deploy RL policies on them. The key thing to check is low-level access: you want to send joint position targets or torques directly, not just velocity commands through the manufacturer's controller, because the whole point is to run your own learned policy.

So my recommendation: simulation first, then a small, robust quadruped with good low-level access and an active community. Once sim-to-real works on that, moving to more complex platforms is much easier.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a quadruped because it is less likely to break when it falls, and says that matters when testing policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually say you don't need a physical robot at all to start. The best entry point is in simulation. Pick up something like Isaac Gym or Isaac Lab, grab a quadruped model, and start training walking policies from scratch. That's where you learn the real lessons: reward shaping, domain randomization, how the observation space affects learning, why your robot falls over in weird ways. You can iterate thousands of times a day there, which you never get with hardware.

If you do want hardware, a quadruped is the right choice. Legged locomotion is where RL has clearly beaten classical control, so you get a very rewarding sim-to-real loop. The Unitree platforms are what I'd point to. The Go1 and Go2 are relatively affordable, they're robust enough to survive your early policies falling over, and the community support is huge. There are open-source training pipelines and deployment code already out there, so you can go from a trained policy to the real robot walking in a reasonable amount of time.

I'd steer away from starting with a humanoid or a biped. The dynamics are much less forgiving, the hardware is expensive, and every fall costs you. Learn the fundamentals on four legs first. Once you've got a quadruped walking reliably on rough terrain, you'll have a much better intuition for what's actually hard, and then you can move to more challenging platforms.

r001.rationale: It recommends Unitree quadrupeds as robust enough to survive early policies falling over, directly identifying fall survival as a robot-selection consideration.

astra-6.text: I would start in simulation. You can learn a lot about locomotion reinforcement learning without having to deal with the hardware at the same time. A quadruped is a good starting point because balancing is easier than with a biped, so you can focus on getting the training pipeline working and understanding the rewards. Then, if you want to move to a real robot, I’d look for a small quadruped with a good software interface and an existing simulation model.

r001.rationale: The response recommends simulation and a quadruped with a good software interface, but does not mention surviving falls without breaking as a robot-selection consideration.

sol-6.1.text: I would start in simulation. Pick a simple quadruped with an existing model and a working reinforcement learning example. That lets you focus on the basics—observations, actions, rewards, and how the policy learns to walk—without having to deal with hardware problems at the same time. Once you have that working and understand the training process, you can think about transferring it to a real robot.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with a simulated quadruped but does not say that a robot should be able to survive falls without breaking.
